quote: Suche die Invariante einer Punktmenge d.h. wie kann ich [-für einen beliebig gegeb. Punkt-] ein allgemeines Gesetz finden, d.h. von vorneherein definiren, welches mir ge- stattet aus jeder beliebig gegebenen Punktmenge einen bestimmten Punkt herauszugreifen.
english: Seek the invariant of a point set, i.e. how can I find a general law, i.e. define in advance one that allows me to pick out a definite point from any arbitrarily given point set.
topic: Methodological aphorisms on problem solving, creativity versus criticism, a proposed problem of choosing a distinguished point from an arbitrary point set, the role of the Archimedean axiom in geometry and physics, the group concept, and classifying ideas by method.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert asks for a uniform rule, fixed in advance, that picks out one definite point from every nonempty set of points, for example every nonempty subset of R or R^n. In modern terms this is a choice function on the power set of the continuum minus the empty set. It is equivalent to a well-ordering of the continuum, since such an ordering picks the least element of each set. His word 'define' turns this into a sharper question: can such a selector or well-ordering be explicitly definable, and not just shown to exist?
triage.answered_by: Ernst Zermelo showed in 1904, in a letter to Hilbert himself, that such a rule exists. He introduced the choice principle (the axiom of choice) and used it to prove that every set can be well-ordered. Whether the rule can be defined explicitly was settled by independence results in the 1960s. Building on Cohen's forcing method, Feferman (1965) showed that in Cohen's model there is no set-theoretically definable well-ordering of the reals. Levy added results on the same model. Gödel's earlier constructible universe L shows the other side: there a definable well-ordering of the reals does exist. So ZFC proves that a choice rule exists but cannot prove that a definable one exists.

evidence.claim: Zermelo published a proof of the well-ordering theorem in 1904, as an extract from a letter to Hilbert, where he first introduced the 'choice' principle.
On 24 September 1904 Zermelo sent Hilbert a letter proving the well-ordering theorem from what he later called the axiom of choice.
The well-ordering theorem is equivalent to the axiom of choice.
Feferman showed that in Cohen's model, obtained by adding a Cohen real to a model of V=L, there is no set-theoretically definable well-ordering of the reals.

triage.why: The note asks almost word for word for a choice function on point sets. That is the problem behind the well-ordering of the continuum, which Hilbert also raised as part of his 1st Paris problem in 1900; I recall this rather than having a source for it, and I found no source linking this page to that problem. Zermelo answered the question of existence in a letter to Hilbert in 1904. Whether a definable rule exists was shown to be independent of ZFC in the 1960s: no in Feferman's work on Cohen's model, yes in Gödel's L. Definable well-orderings of the reals are still studied in descriptive and inner-model set theory, but no source I found describes that as an active open problem, so I marked active_today as unclear. Confidence is medium because the diary note cannot be dated, so I can't tell whether it was written before or after Zermelo's 1904 proof.
